extracted.intended_audience: regulatory practitioners, small business advocates, law students, and members of the general public interested in U.S. administrative law and rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and statutory requirements for how federal agencies must assess and address the impacts of proposed and existing regulations on small entities under the Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) and related laws/orders. Covers procedural steps, analyses to publish, oversight mechanisms, and special provisions (e.g., SBREFA, E.O.13272).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to analyze impact on small entities
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal agencies must analyze the impact of their regulatory actions on small entities (small businesses, small non-profit organizations and small jurisdictions of government). Both current and proposed federal regulations are subject to the RFA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This analysis is a key part of the process for issuing regulations; agencies must assess impacts and include those assessments in required documents (see IRFA/FRFA). The RFA adds management oversight, predictability and transparency to agency rulemaking through these analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trigger for 'significant' impact and requirement to seek less burdensome alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the regulatory impact is likely to be "significant", affecting a "substantial number" of small entities, agencies must seek less burdensome alternatives for them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies are required to select less burdensome alternatives when feasible, or explain the rationale for not doing so. The RFA compels consideration of alternatives but does not require outcome changes to an agency's statutory mission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-fold procedure for seeking less burdensome alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: The process for seeking less burdensome alternatives is three-fold: (1) solicit views of affected small entities; (2) consider the views of the SBA Office of Advocacy; (3) publish an initial regulatory flexibility analysis (IRFA) and/or a final regulatory flexibility analysis (FRFA) in the Federal Register, or provide a certification that the regulation will have no "significant impact."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These steps provide transparency and opportunities for input; publication in the Federal Register or issuance of a certification is required depending on impact. The solicitation and consideration steps are integral to the IRFA/FRFA process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of IRFA/FRFA or certification
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must publish an initial regulatory flexibility analysis (IRFA) and/or a final regulatory flexibility analysis (FRFA) in the Federal Register, or provide a certification that the regulation will have no "significant impact."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishing analyses in the Federal Register ensures public notice and creates a paper trail for judicial review. Certifications are permitted when agencies determine there is no significant impact; improper certification can be challenged in court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solicit views of affected small entities
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must solicit views of affected small entities as part of the RFA process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solicitation occurs during IRFA development and public comment phases; effective solicitation affects the quality of alternatives considered and the defensibility of agency analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of SBA Office of Advocacy views and publication of a response
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must consider the views of the SBA Office of Advocacy. Under E.O.13272, agencies must notify the Office before publishing draft rules expected to have a significant small business impact, consider the Office's written comments on proposed rules, and publish a response with the final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.O.13272 strengthens the role of the Office of Advocacy by requiring vetting of agency policies with the Office and publication of responses to its comments to increase accountability and transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 610 periodic review of existing regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: The RFA requires federal agencies to review all of their existing regulations over a period of ten years and revise those that are duplicative, excessively burdensome, or no longer necessary (Section 610 review).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies publish a plan for Section 610 reviews with the unified agendas. Although often ignored in practice, the ten-year review is intended to reduce unnecessary burdens on small entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unified Agenda publication and indexing of rules affecting small entities
rubrics_metrics.description: The RFA requires government-wide semi-annual regulatory agendas ("unified agendas") that note all planned federal regulations and separately index those expected to "significantly" impact small entities, as well as those that may affect small entities but not "significantly."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unified agendas increase predictability and allow stakeholders to monitor forthcoming rules. They also single out regulations covered by other statutes and executive orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: SBREFA requirement for small business advocacy review panels (EPA and OSHA)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act (SBREFA) mandated that the EPA and OSHA convene small business advocacy review panels to consult with small entities on regulations expected to have a significant impact on them, before those regulations are published for public comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SBREFA both institutionalized direct consultation with small entities for certain agencies and strengthened RFA enforcement by providing judicial review; the panel requirement is an early, pre-notice consultation for significant-impact rules at EPA and OSHA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial review of agency compliance with the RFA
rubrics_metrics.description: SBREFA (1996) gave the courts jurisdiction to review agency compliance with the RFA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial review enables enforcement of RFA's procedural requirements. Court decisions have on occasion suspended agency regulations for failure to comply with RFA procedures; the focus is on process fidelity rather than imposing substantive outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: E.O.13272 requirements for agency procedures, notifications, and training
rubrics_metrics.description: Executive Order 13272 requires federal agencies to establish written procedures and policies explaining how they measure the impact of their regulatory proposals on small entities, to vet those policies with the Office of Advocacy, to notify the Office before publishing draft rules expected to have a significant small business impact, and to consider and respond to the Office's written comments with the final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.O.13272 also requires the Office of Advocacy to provide notification and training to agencies on RFA compliance; agencies complied by submitting written plans and making RFA procedures publicly available. The Office set up mechanisms (e.g., an email address, compliance guide) to facilitate notification and training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of entities covered by the RFA
rubrics_metrics.description: The RFA's coverage includes small businesses, small nonprofit organizations, and small governmental jurisdictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Act's intent is to fit regulatory requirements to the scale of the businesses, organizations, and governmental jurisdictions subject to regulation, and to solicit and consider flexible regulatory proposals for those entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: RFA as a procedural (not substantive) requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The RFA requires agencies to assess impacts and to select less burdensome alternatives or explain why they cannot, but it does not compel specific regulatory outcomes or require agencies to alter their statutory missions or legal mandates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts enforcing the RFA focus on whether agencies followed required procedures and provided adequate explanations; remedies usually address procedural defects rather than ordering particular substantive regulatory results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office of Advocacy monitoring and enforcement roles
rubrics_metrics.description: The SBA Office of Advocacy is tasked with monitoring agency compliance with the RFA, reporting annually to the President and the Congress, filing amicus curiae briefs in appeals brought by small entities, and providing guidance and training to agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office of Advocacy also developed RFA compliance guides, training materials, and notification mechanisms to assist agencies. Its annual reports track compliance and estimate regulatory cost impacts on small entities.
